name: resonant_originality
what_it_measures: Whether the script feels fresh in a way that also lands immediately — not just novel, but surprising AND inevitable in hindsight. The feeling of 'I've never seen this, but of course this exists.'
strong_signals: A premise or approach that feels genuinely new yet requires zero explanation to grasp
Formal or structural choices that feel daring but earned — risky without being alienating
A voice or angle that could only come from this specific creative sensibility, yet is universally legible
Moments that surprise you but feel retrospectively obvious — the 'why didn't anyone do this before?' quality
weak_signals: Bold or weird in ways that confuse rather than intrigue — risky but not landing
Novel premise that requires too much explanation or warm-up before it clicks
Competent execution of a familiar form with minor twists — safe originality
Originality that feels imported or grafted on rather than organic to the material

anchors.9-10: Breaking Bad: 'chemistry teacher becomes meth cook' is completely original yet instantly obvious why it works. The Wire: institutional crime drama from the inside is a totally fresh lens that clicks immediately.
anchors.7-8: The Americans: fresh spy-genre angle (sleeper agents as married couple) is novel and intriguing but takes a beat to fully land. Fleabag: fourth-wall direct address feels fresh yet immediately natural.
anchors.5-6: A procedural with one unusual setting or hook — feels new enough to get made but not genuinely surprising. Genre mashup that's interesting but doesn't feel inevitable.
anchors.3-4: Derivative premise with surface-level freshness — one unusual casting choice or setting on an otherwise familiar show.
anchors.1-2: Pure imitation of existing shows with no distinguishing angle. Feels like a pitch that starts 'it's X meets Y.'

name: world_density_and_texture
what_it_measures: How rich, layered, and story-generating the world feels. Strong scripts imply a setting, social ecosystem, or environment with enough depth and specificity to support years of storytelling — not just a backdrop but an engine.
strong_signals: The world has clear rules, hierarchies, and tensions that create ongoing story potential
Secondary characters and institutions feel like they have full lives beyond what we see
The setting itself generates story — geography, social structure, or context creates conflict naturally
Specific, granular details that make the world feel lived-in and real rather than generic
The pilot implies a large off-screen world with visible edges and interesting gaps
weak_signals: The setting is purely functional — a backdrop with no inherent story energy
World feels generic and interchangeable with any other show in the genre
No sense of ecosystem or social texture — characters exist in a vacuum
Rules of the world are vague or inconsistent
Limited sense that there are other stories happening beyond our protagonists

anchors.9-10: The Wire: Baltimore's institutional ecosystem is so dense the show ran 5 seasons without repeating. The Sopranos: New Jersey mob world has social hierarchy, ritual, geography — every element generates story.
anchors.7-8: Mad Men: the ad agency world of the 1960s has dense social rules and texture. Game of Thrones: the Westeros political ecosystem is explicitly rich with competing families and history.
anchors.5-6: A procedural set in a specific profession — the world has some texture but is mostly a container for cases. The world is specific enough to recognize but doesn't generate story independently.
anchors.3-4: Generic suburban or urban setting with no distinctive social texture. Characters could exist in almost any context.
anchors.1-2: Completely featureless setting — the world has no discernible texture, rules, or story-generating capacity.

name: tonal_specificity
what_it_measures: How distinct and hard-to-imitate the script's tonal identity feels. Strong scripts have a clear emotional, comedic, or dramatic signature that is immediately recognizable and could not be easily replicated by a different team.
strong_signals: A consistent tonal register that is immediately recognizable — you could identify this show from a single scene
The tone blends elements (dark comedy, warmth under cynicism, absurdism with emotional stakes) in a ratio that feels unique to this show
Tonal choices feel confident and specific — not hedging between registers
The comedic or dramatic 'flavor' is distinct from other shows in the same genre
The pilot establishes a clear emotional contract with the audience — you know exactly what kind of show this is
weak_signals: Tone feels generic — could be any network drama or sitcom
Uncertain or hedging between registers in ways that feel unintentional rather than deliberate
The show's emotional signature is interchangeable with dozens of similar shows
Tonal inconsistencies that feel like a lack of creative control rather than intentional complexity
The vibe is correct for the genre but not specific to this show

anchors.9-10: Fleabag: a specific blend of raw grief, dark comedy, and direct emotional intimacy that is completely unmistakable. Atlanta: surrealist Black Southern absurdism with genuine menace — instantly identifiable tonal fingerprint.
anchors.7-8: Succession: a specific flavor of cringe-comedy-tragedy for the ultra-wealthy. The Good Place: warm philosophical sitcom with precise comic timing — distinct but more legible.
anchors.5-6: A well-executed genre show with consistent tone but nothing that distinguishes it from the field. Solid drama or comedy that nails the expected register without adding anything new.
anchors.3-4: Inconsistent or generic tone — feels like it's still figuring out what kind of show it wants to be. The emotional register is familiar and underdeveloped.
anchors.1-2: No tonal identity — mood shifts arbitrarily, or the show adopts a completely generic register with no personality.

name: latent_depth_slow_burn_potential
what_it_measures: Whether the pilot suggests deeper long-term payoff even if restrained or understated on first pass. Strong scripts imply hidden reserves of character, thematic, or world depth that will reward continued viewing — the sense that there is much more beneath the surface.
strong_signals: Characters who reveal one layer in the pilot but clearly have several more waiting
Thematic or philosophical undercurrents that are present but not over-explained
Scenes or details that feel richer on a second viewing than the first
A world or situation where you can sense unexplored corners and future complications
Restrained execution that feels confident — holds back not because it's empty but because it's patient
weak_signals: Everything on the surface — the pilot shows its full hand immediately with no sense of reserves
Characters fully explained in the pilot with no apparent deeper layers
Themes stated explicitly rather than implied — nothing left for the audience to discover
Frenetic pilot that front-loads excitement but implies nothing deeper beneath
No sense that the show will reveal more about itself over time

anchors.9-10: Schitt's Creek: pilot appears to be a fish-out-of-water comedy but contains seeds of a show about family love and human decency that fully bloom three seasons in. Mad Men: the pilot reveals Don Draper's surface but the depth of his reinvented identity takes seasons to excavate.
anchors.7-8: Severance: the pilot is deliberately withholding — you sense enormous depth but see only the surface. The Americans: restraint in the pilot implies deep character reservoirs ahead.
anchors.5-6: A pilot with some character mystery or unresolved subtext that suggests more depth than average procedural, but the show's ceiling feels visible from the start.
anchors.3-4: Thin pilot where what you see is what you get. Characters and world feel fully exhausted after one episode.
anchors.1-2: Completely surface-level — no sense of any depth beneath what is shown. The pilot implies this is as complex as the show will get.

name: relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine
what_it_measures: How much recurring story energy exists in the relationships between characters. Strong scripts create multiple durable interpersonal dynamics — not just a protagonist with satellites, but a web of relationships that can independently generate conflict, comedy, and evolution across seasons.
strong_signals: Multiple character relationships that each have their own distinct dynamic and story potential
The ensemble creates a system where any two characters in a room together generate material
Relationship tensions are structural rather than episodic — will still be present in season 3
Power dynamics, history, and competing desires between characters that are durable, not one-time
Secondary relationships (not just protagonist-centered) that feel generative and interesting
weak_signals: Protagonist-centric with thin relationships to functional satellites
Relationships established in the pilot feel resolved or exhaustible — no durable tension
Characters primarily defined by their relationship to the lead rather than to each other
Ensemble present but interchangeable — relationships lack distinct flavor
The show could sustain a season on plot alone, with characters as vehicles rather than engines

anchors.9-10: Seinfeld: the four leads have entirely distinct dynamics with each other — George/Jerry is different from Elaine/Jerry is different from Kramer/George — infinite combinatorial energy. The Office: the ensemble web is so rich that even secondary characters like Kevin and Angela generate their own storylines.
anchors.7-8: Parks and Recreation: the ensemble creates a system where any subset of characters generates material. Modern Family: three family units with distinct dynamics that can be combined endlessly.
anchors.5-6: A procedural with a solid lead-partner dynamic and decent supporting cast — enough ensemble to sustain seasons but not a full generative web.
anchors.3-4: Protagonist and 2-3 thin relationships. The show lives or dies on the lead alone. Supporting characters are functional.
anchors.1-2: Solo protagonist or relationships so thin they do not constitute an ensemble engine. All story energy comes from plot, not character dynamics.
